description: Article chain detection. A boundary is the adjacent page pair (N, N+1); its endpoints are drawn from the last paragraph of page N and the first paragraph of page N+1 in derived reading order. Eligibility is read per endpoint: the tail endpoint answers to the chain_eligible policy of page N and the head endpoint to that of page N+1, so a page the vocabulary keeps out of chains withdraws only its own end of the boundary. The mask is a qualification, not a term in the score. A paragraph set narrower than chain_endpoint_min_width_ratio of the page is a fragment beside the text rather than part of it -- a byline, a credit, a boxed aside -- and never stands in for the page's last or first paragraph. Each signal named by a weight_<signal> key returns a value in 0..1, and the boundary score is the weighted sum over the signals divided by the total positive weight, clamped to 0..1; a signal the geometry cannot supply contributes nothing. A negative weight is a soft prior that withdraws evidence rather than supplying any, so it stays out of the denominator, and the loader refuses a weight set in which a boundary carrying every signal at full strength could be pulled below link_min_score by the priors alone. That refusal is what keeps paragraph level evidence authoritative over the page level prior. pair_classes declares the kinds of handover a boundary may carry: a class is a set of layout labels, a pairing names the tail class and the head class it joins, and each pairing weighs the signals its own way, starting from the flat weights and replacing what it declares. Every allowed pairing that finds both its endpoints is scored and the boundary takes the strongest. terminal_punctuation lists the sentence enders, Latin and CJK, and terminal_closers the closing marks stripped from a tail before its ender is read, so a quoted sentence still reads as ended; both are written as JSON unicode escapes to keep this file ASCII. A boundary also exists inside one page, between one column and the next: a magazine sets three columns to a sheet and a sentence broken between the second and the third is a handover of exactly the same kind as one broken across a page break. boundary_kinds names the two kinds, and boundary_priority declares the order chain assembly takes them in, which matters because assembly is exclusive: a paragraph is the tail of at most one edge and the head of at most one, so where two edges want the same end the earlier kind in this list wins and the later is dropped. column_adjacent pairs band n with band n+1; body_next pairs band n with band n+2, which is the handover hidden behind a band offering no endpoint the pair rules take -- a display line set in its own band between two text columns is such a band. body_next is last in the priority because a skipped band that did have an endpoint means the adjacent edge is the real handover and the skipping edge is redundant. Two of the six signals cannot mean inside a page what they mean across a page break, and both are handled by saying so: column_position asks whether the tail sits at the foot of the last column and the head at the head of the first, which the in-page pairing makes true by construction, so it enters as the constant 1 and its share of the score is reported separately; and opener_prior is the prior that a page declared to start an article does start one, which a column declares nothing about, so it is zero. A seventh signal, whether the tail ends on a hyphen, is recorded and not scored, because its weight has never been calibrated and an uncalibrated term would make the total say more than the calibration behind it. Two page level policy flags qualify a column boundary. preserve_line_structure says the page sets records one to a line, and a page of records hands nothing over between its columns, so it yields no column boundary at all. chain_eligible is deliberately not read here: it answers whether running text continues into or out of a page, which is a question about a page break and not about a handover internal to one page. column_head_block_classes and head_clear_gap_em are the fourth gate: a column head with a display line set within head_clear_gap_em of its own type size directly above it is not the top of a column of running text, it is the first line under a heading, and the column before it hands over to nothing. The classes named there must be declared endpoint classes, so the gate reads the same vocabulary the scoring does. Retune the weights and thresholds here from the report produced by tools/chain_report.py, never in code. intra_column is the third boundary kind: two bands of running text stacked inside one column, the shape a wrap around a photo or pull quote leaves. Its rule is deterministic rather than scored -- consecutive body-labelled candidates of one band, horizontally overlapping, vertical gap within intra_column_chain_max_gap_pt, the tail free of terminal punctuation, the head clear -- so its rows carry the measured signals and a null score. It stands last in boundary_priority: where an in-page stack and a column or page handover want the same endpoint, the cross-boundary evidence wins.

pair_classes.description: The kinds of handover a boundary may carry. classes maps a class name to the layout labels that belong to it, every one of which must also be an endpoint candidate. pairs declares which class may hand over to which; a combination not declared here is not a handover this detector recognises and is never scored. A pairing may replace any weight_<signal> default under weights, bounded by the range the flat weight declares. The running text pairing keeps the flat weights. The display line pairing weighs what a broken heading can actually show: it stops without an ender and it is set in the same type as the line completing it. It cannot fill a measure, because a single line paragraph has none, and it is not running text, so those two weigh nothing rather than counting against it.
